rationale: A wins because it finds the reporter question that turns this from a vendor announcement into a story: 'Airtable is shipping agents that act on enterprise data - and won't say how often they get it right.' B is competent, but it spends too much space remapping markets with lines like 'The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market - Airtable is the data point.' A is sharper because it makes the undisclosed reliability data the risk, not a housekeeping footnote.
gaps_in_A: 'The prevailing belief is that 2025-26's selling point for enterprise AI is autonomy' is plausible, but it is outside the supplied facts and needs sourcing before it carries weight.
'a bad draft sent' overreaches slightly: the update says agents draft emails, not that they send them.
'category that already has incumbents' is a good shape, but the angle stays abstract until a real incumbent or analyst contrast is supplied.
'Draft one tight pitch around it' is a half-step premature; the reliability angle should first get Airtable's on-record answer or refusal.
gaps_in_B: It buries the best story as a question: 'Is Airtable willing to share any reliability or error-rate data on the agents?' That should have been an angle, not cleanup.
'all-in product pivot to AI agents' overstates the update. Repositioning is supplied; all-in is theater.

'The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market' and 'Airtable just entered the AI agent market' are too close. One is category, one is competitive, but both are market-map wrappers.
'what the pivot means for the path to liquidity' invents a finance frame the update does not give. Valuation pressure is fair; liquidity is not.
